items.title: GitLab Orbit is GA: Higher agent accuracy, lower token cost
items.summary: An agent’s true cost isn’t only the tokens it burns. It’s the review that calls your code “safe to merge” after seeing the diff, but without any context on the pipeline. We call that artificial confidence, not artificial intelligence. Agents guess because code is all they can see; they can’t see the merge request that last changed it, the pipeline that ran it, the vulnerability it carries, or the people who wrote and reviewed it.Guessing is expensive. If you’ve tried running agents in a large monorepo, one with tens of thousands of files, you know how it goes: the agent iterates, pinging the backend again and again for the information it needs to complete the task. Every round trip costs more time and more tokens. Eventually the agent gives up.The model isn’t the constraint. Context is.That’s the constraint that GitLab Orbit removes. Now generally available, Orbit is the context graph for your software lifecycle: a live, queryable view of all your code, merge requests, work items, pipelines, vulnerabilities, and ownership, with every relationship continuously updated as you ship. Every agent and engineer can work from one connected view of the lifecycle. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit needed up to 45x fewer retries and used 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model.Grounded agents get answers right the first timeAn agent like Claude Code, connected to GitLab Orbit through MCP, stops crawling files and instead asks the graph. The first response comes back with real callers, recent changes, and owners, so your follow-up prompts can refine the answer rather than correct it. The difference is measurable. Compare the Market, one of the UK’s largest price comparison platforms, tested four context approaches for an internal AI code reviewer across 79 real merge requests. The GitLab Orbit-grounded reviewer matched about 70% of expected inline comments; RAG managed about 58%, worse than no added context at all.“GitLab Orbit gave us an AI code reviewer that actually understands our codebase, not just the diff in front of it. We tested it against RAG and a few other approaches across real merge requests, and the gap was clear. Better comment placement, better summaries of what actually changed.”— Ryan Harvey, Head of AI Engineering, Compare the MarketFewer retries means fewer tokensA recent analysis from a leading research and advisory firm found that the cost of an undisciplined agent session is dominated by retransmitting context that didn’t change between turns. That token cost comes from how the agent is set up, not from the model itself.GitLab Orbit changes that engineering. The agent gets one bounded answer from the graph instead of reloading everything that might matter. In GitLab testing, agents connected to Orbit used up to 4.5x fewer tokens on the same tasks with the same model: each turn carries less context, and fewer turns go to work that never ships. Because the graph is shared, that cost doesn’t repeat per agent. Duo agents, Claude Code, Codex, and your own tools all query the same graph, so the context you build for the first agent is already there for the second.Questions you couldn’t answer beforeSince GitLab Orbit entered beta in June, we’ve worked with design partners running it against real codebases, real incidents, and real merge requests. Their first win was almost always a question they couldn’t get answered before.Here are a few questions design partners asked Orbit that they couldn’t answer before, and what came back:Which production services are exposed to this vulnerability? A single query returns the services that include the component, the merge requests that introduced it, the environments it reached, and the teams that own each one. One design partner answered a security-coverage question across 34 million entities in seven minutes; through the API, the same question would have taken half a day. When a vulnerability lands, security has a complete remediation plan within the hour, not a partial list by the end of the day.What breaks if I change this? Before a push, a developer or their agent can ask which services, jobs, and environments a change touches, across every project in the group, not just the one open in the editor. Review agents bring the same answer to the merge request, so a “safe to merge” comment reflects the whole system instead of the diff. Across 79 real merge requests, Compare the Market’s reviewer flagged more real issues in the right places than their RAG-based version. Problems get caught in review, before they become outages.Why does this CI job keep failing, and where else? GitLab Orbit shows how often a job fails across every project that runs it, which projects have drifted from the shared CI configuration, and who owns them. What used to be a Slack thread asking three teams “has anyone seen this?” becomes one answer. items.title: GitLab Orbit: Find vulnerability blast radius without the manual hunt
items.summary: A critical vulnerability needs a fix and a map. The fix is usually fast. Finding where the vulnerable component lives, who owns it, and whether it's exposed to the Internet is what costs you time. Most security teams piece that answer together from scanner reports, spreadsheets, and a Slack thread asking who owns a service nobody recognizes, and you stay exposed for every hour that takes.GitLab Orbit, now generally available, replaces this manual work with a single query. Orbit connects code, merge requests, pipelines, security findings, and ownership in one graph that stays current as your teams ship. Ask which projects are affected and who owns them, and you get an answer in minutes. Agents answer from the graph instead of crawling repositories and stitching together API calls, so they need fewer retries and fewer tokens to get there.Why scanners alone can't answer the questionPHP2Shell, the set of critical PHP flaws disclosed last week, illustrates the problem. PHP is usually installed as a system package, compiled from source, or baked into a container image, not managed as an application dependency. Vulnerable versions can sit on web servers, in container images, in old CI jobs, or in internal tools nobody remembers building. The fix was a version upgrade. Finding every affected installation took time.Security tools provide different views of the environment. Dependency scanning identifies vulnerable application dependencies. Container scanning detects vulnerabilities in operating system packages, language dependencies, and other software components. Code search helps locate where images and configurations are referenced. But identifying a vulnerability is only part of the job. Teams still need to know which services are affected, who owns them, which pipelines build and deploy them, and where to apply the fix. That information is often spread across multiple systems.That leaves your team to connect the dots, each holding a different piece. Your security engineer can assess the severity but may not see every affected system. Your platform engineer owns the base images and CI templates that hundreds of projects depend on, but can't see every project that uses them. Your developers get pulled off their roadmap to search repositories for a component they may not know they own. Your CISO has to tell leadership whether the company is exposed before anyone has a full list.An attacker only needs to find one vulnerable system. You need to find all of them. Exploiting a vulnerability is now the most common way breaches begin, at 31% in Verizon's 2026 report, and the same report found attackers using generative AI at several stages of an attack. The map needs to exist before the advisory lands.A first-party graph of your entire SDLCOrbit draws on the data GitLab already runs on: your merge requests, pipelines, deployments, and vulnerabilities. A CVE in Orbit's graph connects directly to the services, pipelines, environments, and teams it touches. Because the graph is first-party, there's no second system to keep in sync and no new instrumentation to stand up.Without Orbit, an agent or analyst can usually find the vulnerable code but not the full exposure. Someone assembles that picture by hand, tool by tool, and the gaps show up as the long tail of services nobody checked. With Orbit, one query maps the CVE to the services, pipelines, environments, and owners that depend on it, and the output is a scoped, prioritized list your security team can act on.Agents without Orbit hit the same wall: they can't see the whole system, so they guess. In GitLab's testing on the same tasks with the same model, agents running through Orbit were up to 11 times faster, used up to 4.5 times fewer tokens, and needed up to 45 times fewer retries. During an incident, faster answers arrive while the team is still triaging, lower token use keeps queries across a large group from becoming a cost problem, and fewer retries mean your team can act on the first answer instead of re-running the question.Watch the demo to learn how GitLab Orbit can help you understand your exposure:  One graph that connects a CVE to its ownerBlast radius is how far a vulnerability reaches: which projects contain the flawed component, how it got there, who owns those projects, and what changed recently. GitLab already holds most of those facts in separate places, and Orbit connects them. Turn it on for a top-level group, and Orbit indexes projects, merge requests, pipelines, work items, security findings, and source code into one graph of how they relate.From there, you ask in plain language instead of correlating systems by hand: which projects use this library, which merge requests brought it in, and who owns each project? An agent traverses the graph and answers from indexed project data, and you can audit the graph queries behind each answer.Access follows the roles you've already set, so people and agents see only what they're permitted to see.
